name: Visual Genome
description: Visual Genome is a dataset connecting language and vision using crowdsourced dense image annotations. It contains over 108,249 images, each annotated with an average of 21 objects, 18 attributes, and 18 pairwise relationships between objects. The dataset includes region descriptions, objects, attributes, relationships, region graphs, scene graphs, and question-answer pairs. All objects, attributes, relationships, and noun phrases are canonicalized to WordNet synsets. The dataset contains 4,102,818 object instances, 1,773,258 question-answer pairs, and over 1.8 million relationships, making it the densest and largest dataset of image descriptions, objects, attributes, relationships, and question answers.
creator: Ranjay Krishna, Yuke Zhu, Oliver Groth, Justin Johnson, Kenji Hata, Joshua Kravitz, Stephanie Chen, Yannis Kalantidis, Li-Jia Li, David A. Shamma, Michael S. Bernstein, Li Fei-Fei
publisher: Stanford University, Yahoo Inc., Snapchat Inc., Dresden University of Technology
citeAs: Krishna, R., Zhu, Y., Groth, O., Johnson, J., Hata, K., Kravitz, J., Chen, S., Kalantidis, Y., Li, L.-J., Shamma, D. A., Bernstein, M. S., & Fei-Fei, L. (2016). Visual Genome: Connecting Language and Vision Using Crowdsourced Dense Image Annotations. arXiv:1602.07332.
rai:dataCollection: Visual Genome was collected and verified entirely by crowd workers from Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT). The dataset was collected over the course of 6 months after 15 months of experimentation and iteration on the data representation. Approximately 800,000 Human Intelligence Tasks (HITs) were launched on AMT, where each HIT involved creating descriptions, questions and answers, or region graphs. Each HIT was designed such that workers earn anywhere between $6-$8 per hour. The pipeline involved multiple stages for each component: region descriptions, objects, attributes, relationships, region graphs, scene graphs, and question-answer pairs.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The Visual Genome dataset uses 108,249 images from the intersection of the YFCC100M (Thomee et al., 2016) and MS-COCO (Lin et al., 2014). These images are real-world, non-iconic images that were uploaded onto Flickr by users.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: 6 months of data collection after 15 months of experimentation and iteration on the data representation.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: All objects, attributes, relationships, and noun phrases in region descriptions and question-answer pairs are canonicalized to WordNet synsets. Stanford NLP tools are used to extract noun phrases, which are then mapped to their most frequent matching synset in WordNet. Hand-crafted mapping rules are applied for common failure cases (30 rules for objects, 15 for attributes, 20 for relationships). Workers on AMT verify and correct canonicalization mappings. Scene graphs are constructed by merging region graphs, combining co-referenced objects with bounding box overlap over union of 0.8.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Region descriptions are preprocessed by removing all non-alphanumeric characters, lowercasing, and stripping excess whitespace. Attributes are lowercased, lemmatized, and stripped of excess whitespace. BLEU score thresholds (set to 0.7) are used to ensure diversity in region descriptions. Bounding boxes must satisfy coverage and quality requirements. Stanford's dependency parser is used to extract nouns automatically as suggestions for object extraction. Objects from different region graphs are merged if their bounding boxes have an overlap over union of 0.8.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations were collected through Amazon Mechanical Turk in multiple stages. For region descriptions: workers draw bounding boxes and write descriptions, with subsequent workers encouraged to write descriptions not previously written, enforced via BLEU score thresholds. For objects: workers extract objects from descriptions and draw bounding boxes satisfying coverage and quality requirements. For attributes and relationships: workers add attributes to objects and connect pairs of objects with relationships based on region description text. For scene graphs: workers confirm co-referenced objects across region graphs. For QA pairs: workers write freeform QAs (8 pairs per image, at least 3 different W-types) and region-based QAs. All annotations go through verification via majority voting (3 workers, 2 must agree) or rapid judgments for objects.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: All Visual Genome data go through a verification stage. Majority voting involves three unique workers voting on each annotation; an annotation is added if at least two out of three workers verify it as correct. Rapid judgments (inspired by rapid serial visual processing) are used for object verification. Canonicalization precision and recall are evaluated on held-out test sets: Objects (Precision: 88.0%, Recall: 98.5%), Attributes (Precision: 85.7%, Recall: 95.9%), Relationships (Precision: 92.9%, Recall: 88.5%). Visual Genome HITs achieved a 94.1% retention rate.
rai:annotationsPerItem: Average of 42 region descriptions per image, 21 objects per image, 16 attributes per image, 18 relationships per image, and 17 question-answer pairs per image.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 33,000 unique workers contributed. Geographic distribution: United States (93.02%), Philippines (1.29%), Kenya (1.13%), India (0.94%), Russia (0.50%), Canada (0.47%), Others (2.65%). Age range: 18 to 68 years old, with the majority between 25 and 34 years old. Gender: 54.15% male and 45.85% female.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Stanford dependency parser (Manning et al., 2014) used to extract nouns automatically as suggestions for object extraction. Stanford NLP tools used to extract noun phrases for canonicalization. word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) used for semantic analysis of descriptions. BLEU score (Papineni et al., 2002) used to enforce diversity in region descriptions.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The paper refers to the first release of the Visual Genome dataset. Further visualizations, API, and additional information are available at https://visualgenome.org. No explicit versioning, update schedule, or deprecation policy is described in the paper.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset contains images of people with annotations including gender-related attributes (e.g., man, woman, boy, girl), age-related attributes, states of motion, and activities. Annotator demographics including age, gender, and geographic location were collected.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to enable cognitive computer vision tasks such as image description, question answering, and scene understanding. It is intended to advance models that can understand interactions and relationships between objects in images, enabling applications such as image search, question answering, and robotic interactions.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset is somewhat biased towards images of people, as the top synsets include humans playing sports. There is also a bias towards certain sports (skiing, surfboarding) in the image set, which affects attribute distributions. The dataset uses images from the intersection of YFCC100M and MS-COCO, which may introduce biases from those sources. 93.02% of crowd workers contributed from the United States, which may introduce linguistic and cultural biases in annotations.
rai:dataLimitations: Canonicalization mappings are not perfect and still contain some ambiguity. The dataset's region descriptions have a maximum of 16 words. Some descriptions like 'it is a sunny day' contain no objects and therefore have no region graphs. The canonicalization method is not directly comparable to existing WSD benchmarks due to open vocabulary and no annotated ground truth. Relationship classification shows low accuracy (8.74% top-1) due to high intra-class variability.
rai:dataUseCases: Training and benchmarking computer vision models for: attribute prediction, relationship prediction, region description generation, visual question answering, dense image captioning, semantic image retrieval, scene graph generation, image understanding evaluation, relationship extraction, and action recognition.
